title_original: In Deauville, Four Generations Blowin’ in the Wind
excerpt_original: For its seventeenth edition, the Planches Contact festival has gathered sixteen photographers along the Normandy coast under the theme “Generations.” Bruce Gilden, Cristina de Middel, Newsha Tavakolian and Alain Keler rub shoulders with the winners of the young photography…

blocks.text: The gusts forecast for opening weekend are pushing seventy-five miles an hour. Camille Binelli, who runs the festival’s photography department, is unruffled: “On the beach, it’ll hold.” Philippe Augier — the mayor of Deauville and president of Les Franciscaines, the cultural center that houses most of the exhibitions — is no more impressed. “This town has been married to photography since the day it was born,” he says.

The marriage has had its memorable episodes. In August 1951, Robert Capa set his trunks down on the boardwalk on assignment for Holiday , the American travel magazine, which was, in effect, footing the bill for his vacation. “He spent two months here,” the mayor notes, “and the women of Deauville never got over it, the party was that hot.”

That same summer, Magnum’s co-founder set in motion one of the agency’s first great collective undertakings. Eleven photographers, Henri Cartier-Bresson and Eve Arnold among them, divided up fourteen countries across five continents. Armed with a single questionnaire, they asked twenty- to twenty-five-year-olds about their daily lives, their dreams and their fears. Do you have a telephone at home? What do you think of the United Nations? How many children do you want?

“Generation X, as in the unknown generation, the one that came after the war,” explains Lionel Charrier, photo editor at Libération , who co-directs the festival with Jonas Tebib. The series ran in France in December 1952, in the magazine Point de vue, Images du monde . It resurfaces now in Deauville, flanked by two contemporary answers to it on Generation Z, in a room called — you could not make this up — Le Point de Vue.

blocks.text: One of those answers, “Country-Side,” comes from Bruce Gilden, a fixture of American street photography and a Magnum member since 1998. The photographer, who turned eighty the day before the opening, put hundreds of miles of Normandy farmland behind him, stopping at farms, agricultural fairs and one village fête to meet apprentices, students and farmers’ children between thirteen and thirty.

Down on the sand, the thirty-nine outsize prints of his New York retrospective add up to what Charrier calls “one of the largest exhibitions of the American photographer’s work in France.” “It was pretty funny, putting all that seventies New York fauna out on this beach,” he says, standing in front of the flash-lit portraits, where the grotesque surfaces with tenderness. The book that came out of those pictures, Coney Island , has been out of print for years. “Everybody fights over that book, and here you have it, on the beach, supersized.”

The other Magnum commission takes us out to the Cotentin. Cristina de Middel — who chaired the agency from 2022 to 2025 and has built her whole body of work on the porous border between documentary and fiction — settled in one of the most heavily nuclearized territories on the planet, where the “Aval du futur” program, announced in March 2024, promises the largest industrial project in the world. Residents learned about it from the press. To photograph the young people there, in “Les Atomiques de Cherbourg,” she went looking for the sets of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg : the station, the platform, Jacques Demy’s saturated color.

Back in Deauville, facing the sea, stand Tina Merandon’s arresting portraits of dogs and their owners; she holds a grant from the photo4food foundation. The French photographer has spent a decade on the bond between humans and animals. “Soudain la mêlée” catches the scrum itself, fur against skin. “A pack is a little frightening, and at the same time it’s very powerful,” she says. “I like it when things are moving all the time.” The hang melts into the landscape so completely that you lose track of where it stops: past the last frame, dogs off the leash are barreling down the sand.

blocks.text: At Les Franciscaines, the family drawers come open. Newsha Tavakolian, the Iranian photographer and Magnum member, has been photographing her country since she was sixteen. Her off-site residency was to be devoted to the young people of Tehran, and then the war broke out. Worried for her, Charrier offered her a way out. “She told me: no, no, I really want to document my country.” What she brought instead was forty-six glass plates inherited from a distant Kurdish great-uncle, and then her grandfather’s photographs. He had to give up the trade because his wife’s family was ashamed to see him walking around with a camera around his neck. Three generations of intimate images, her own among them, tell Iran’s transformations in the negative.

In the same space, Alain Keler, eighty-one — one of only two Frenchmen ever to win the W. Eugene Smith Grant — shows across from his son Léo, of the Hors-Format agency. “Souvenirs d’Honfleur” lines up the exhibits from a youth misspent between 1961 and 1964: jukeboxes, pinball machines, foosball tables, night buses, clandestine dashes to the nightclubs of Deauville. “It was an absolute madhouse. I came into my own,” he says, delighted. Sixty years later, he photographed a girl from his class picture at the door of their old lycée. Léo, for his part, collected the cahiers de doléances — the books of grievances drawn up during the Great National Debate of 2019 — and tracked down the Normans who had filled them with their lives, sometimes tragic, and their hopes, often disappointed.

blocks.text: Of the four winners of the Young Photographic Creation Prize, hung in with their elders, Flore Prébay asked family caregivers what they would do with a moment entirely their own. One of them answered: “Me, I’m going under. I can’t take any more.” Her portrait was taken at the bottom of a swimming pool.

Farther on, a wall goes to 100 Years , by the German artist Hans-Peter Feldmann, who died in 2023. On loan from the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, it presents a hundred and one portraits of strangers, from infant to centenarian. It is impossible not to place yourself somewhere on that frieze. “You arrive at your own age and you always find the person too old,” Jonas Tebib says.
On one side of the wall, the years already lived. On the other, the co-artistic director adds, “you can take the measure of the ones you have left.” Visitors have until January 3 to do the math.

blocks.text: “Generations,” the 17th edition of the Planches Contact Festival is on view in Deauville (France) through January 3, 2027.
